channel.title: Ibrahim Alobaid — Articles
channel.description: A complete 16-part engineering guide to voice AI agents: digital audio, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, LLM conversation state, real-time transport, turn detection, interruptions, latency, tools and RAG, security, evaluation and a production capstone.

item.title: Capstone: Engineering a Complete Voice AI Agent — From Browser to Production
item.description: Over the previous 15 articles we covered audio fundamentals, STT, LLMs, TTS, WebRTC, interruptions, tool execution, privacy and production evaluation. This final article puts those pieces together in a fictional scheduling voice assistant that listens in a browser…

item.title: How to Evaluate, Observe, and Deploy a Voice AI Agent
item.description: A voice agent that works in a local demo is not yet ready for real callers. Under real traffic it can lose a WebRTC connection, stall during TTS playback, misread a correction, or repeat an external action after a reconnect.

item.title: Voice AI Security, Privacy & Safety: Trust Boundaries, Consent, and Safe Tools
item.description: A user talks into a microphone, a speech provider transcribes the audio, the model reads documents and conversation history, and a tool can change an external system. Making sure the right user authorized each action, that sensitive data is not kept without need…

item.title: From Conversation to Action: Tools, RAG & Agent Workflows for Voice AI
item.description: When a user asks, “What is your cancellation policy?”, the agent needs reliable evidence. When they say, “Book an appointment at ten tomorrow,” it has to take an action in a real system.

item.title: Robust Voice AI in the Wild: Noise, Echo, Accents & Recovery
item.description: A voice agent that works well with a headset in a quiet demo room can break down once someone uses it near a road, a second person speaks, its own output leaks into the microphone, the user switches languages mid-sentence, or the network drops just as a reservation is being confirmed.

item.title: Voice Agent Latency Engineering: From First Token to First Audible Response
item.description: Your LLM returns its first token quickly and your TTS provider starts sending audio promptly, yet the agent still feels sluggish. This article works out which latency to measure, where the waiting accumulates between the end of the user's speech and the first audible reply…

item.title: When Users Interrupt: Barge-In, Playback State, and Context Synchronization
item.description: When a user starts talking while the agent is still speaking, calling stop() on the audio player is not enough. Asynchronous generation, audio queues, client playback, cancellation, and conversation state all have to be coordinated so the agent never treats unplayed words as spoken.

item.title: How Does a Voice Agent Know When to Listen and When to Reply? VAD, Endpointing & Turn Detection
item.description: A voice agent can tell when its microphone is picking up speech, but that alone does not tell it whether the speaker has finished their thought. This article separates Voice Activity Detection (VAD), endpointing, and turn detection…

item.title: Real-Time Audio Transport for Voice Agents: WebRTC vs WebSockets
item.description: A voice agent with good STT, LLM and TTS models can still feel slow or choppy when its audio arrives late or unevenly, and the cause is often the real-time transport layer. This article compares WebRTC and WebSockets for voice agents, explains ICE/STUN/TURN…

item.title: Build Your First Voice Agent with Python and Pipecat: From Components to Conversation
item.description: This article wires speech-to-text (STT), a language model (LLM) and text-to-speech (TTS) into a first browser-based voice agent: you speak into the microphone, and the agent transcribes what you said, generates an answer and speaks it back.

item.title: Choosing a Voice-Agent Architecture: Cascaded vs Speech-to-Speech
item.description: Earlier articles covered how STT turns speech into text, how an LLM writes a response, and how TTS gives that response a voice, but a voice agent does not always need three separately connected models.

item.title: The Voice Agent's Brain: LLMs and Conversation State
item.description: The previous two articles covered how STT transcribes speech and how TTS speaks a reply. Between them sits the large language model (LLM), which works out what the user wants and decides how to answer.

item.title: Text-to-Speech: How to Make a Voice Agent Sound Natural
item.description: In Article 03, we saw how a speech recognizer turns audio into text; this article goes the other way, from the agent's answer to speech that is intelligible, natural, low-latency, and stops when the user interrupts. In a real voice agent, TTS is much more than writing an MP3 file.

item.title: Speech-to-Text: How Machines Turn Spoken Language into Text
item.description: In many voice-agent architectures, “understanding speech” starts with Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), which maps incoming audio to text. That transcript is not an infallible record: it can change while someone is still speaking, and it can get names, dates, numbers, and accented speech wrong.

item.title: Digital Audio for Developers: The Foundation of Every Voice AI Agent
item.description: Before your user's speech reaches a speech recognition model, it has already become numbers. Without a working understanding of sampling, sample rate, bit depth, PCM, channels, chunks, and codecs, you can misinterpret those numbers, feed a model the wrong audio format, or add avoidable latency.

item.title: What Is a Voice AI Agent? From Speech to Natural Conversation
item.description: A Voice AI Agent is an end-to-end interactive system: it receives audio, works out what the user wants, decides what to do next, and answers in speech while managing timing, context, and interruptions. That makes it much more than a speech recognizer or a synthetic voice reading an LLM's answer.
